title: You Can’t Automate What You Can’t Articulate
author: Andrea Chiarelli
summary: Chiarelli argues that as AI takes over drafting and analysis, the enduring human skill is problem framing: deciding what is worth solving before any tool, human or artificial, starts work. She presents it as the core purpose of higher education and, by extension, of anyone who has to set direction. The piece then offers a practical toolkit of four frameworks, E5, PICO, Cynefin and the Fishbone diagram, each with a worked example. She advises trying several in different contexts rather than agonising over the perfect choice, since judgment about which lens fits develops with practice. Her closing claim is that people who frame problems well stay indispensable however capable the technology becomes. I filed it under Leadership because the operative skill is diagnosis and direction-setting in decision-making.
points: Problem framing, not analysis, is the human skill that machines should not and cannot take over.
E5 slows you down to expand, examine assumptions and empathise before any solution is proposed.
PICO and the Fishbone diagram impose precision on a question or a root-cause search, turning a loose complaint into a testable inquiry.
Cynefin warns that clear, complicated, complex and chaotic problems each need a different management style.
Experiment with several frameworks first; the sense of which one fits comes with practice.
quotes: We will always need to teach people to analyse, to frame, to distinguish between a vague impression and a defined challenge. Indeed, these abilities cannot, and arguably should not, be outsourced to machines. We still need people who can weigh competing priorities and set the direction before any tool, human or artificial, can begin to work effectively.

By forcing you to specify these four elements, PICO sharpens your focus. Its disciplined structure is valuable not only in medicine but in any field where there is a risk of drifting into topics that are interesting but unmanageable.

The strength of Cynefin is that it alerts you to the fact that not all problems should be treated alike. Some can be solved with best practice, others require expert judgment and some demand probing, iteration and adaptation.
This process often shifts the problem frame from “builders are careless” to “systemic gaps in design and procurement,” opening the door to more effective solutions.

Early on, the best approach is not to agonise over choosing the perfect method but to try out several. Experiment with E5, PICO, Cynefin and Fishbone in different contexts, and notice which ones yield insights that feel useful. You may discover that one framework helps you open a problem up, while another helps you narrow it down. Some will fit neatly, others less so. The process of testing them is itself part of learning how to frame problems.

The enduring human skill lies in knowing how to identify and articulate challenges worth solving. In a world where information is cheap and abundant, the ability to define meaningful problems is what sets you apart.
